chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Preface The law touches the lives of all Americans.
text_raw:
Preface 
The law touches the lives of all Americans.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Even such common¬ place activities as driving a car, depositing money in a bank, and entering a retail store have legal ramifications, although we are not ordinarily conscious of them.
text_raw:
Even such common¬ 
place activities as driving a car, depositing money in a bank, and 
entering a retail store have legal ramifications, although we are not 
ordinarily conscious of them.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: At other times—as when a relative dies or when we marry or divorce, file our income taxes, are injured in an accident, or sell or purchase a home—we may be acutely aware of the law’s presence.
text_raw:
At other times—as when a relative dies 
or when we marry or divorce, file our income taxes, are injured in 
an accident, or sell or purchase a home—we may be acutely aware 
of the law’s presence.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: At such times we feel the need to know the law and to understand the often unfamiliar terms that make up its language.
text_raw:
At such times we feel the need to know the 
law and to understand the often unfamiliar terms that make up its 
language.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Merriam-WEBSTER’S Dictionary OF Law is designed to meet these needs by offering convenient and comprehensive access to the language of law.
text_raw:
Merriam-WEBSTER’S Dictionary OF Law is designed to meet 
these needs by offering convenient and comprehensive access to the 
language of law.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: It provides concise coverage of more than 10,000 legal words and phrases, based on a thorough examination of the le¬ gally relevant citations drawn from the nearly 15,000,000 citations in the Merriam-Webster offices and supplemented by a review of ma¬ terial available through various on-line legal databases.
text_raw:
It provides concise coverage of more than 10,000 
legal words and phrases, based on a thorough examination of the le¬ 
gally relevant citations drawn from the nearly 15,000,000 citations in 
the Merriam-Webster offices and supplemented by a review of ma¬ 
terial available through various on-line legal databases.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: To make the dictionary easier to use, the information provided here is presented in a style that will be familiar to all users of standard desk dictionaries.
text_raw:
To make the 
dictionary easier to use, the information provided here is presented in 
a style that will be familiar to all users of standard desk dictionaries.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Entries include definitions, pronunciations, variant spellings, gram¬ matical information, etymologies for many words, and other con¬ ventional dictionary features.
text_raw:
Entries include definitions, pronunciations, variant spellings, gram¬ 
matical information, etymologies for many words, and other con¬ 
ventional dictionary features.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: None of this information is intended to substitute for the expertise of a lawyer, but it will help to make encounters with law and lawyers less mysterious.
text_raw:
None of this information is intended 
to substitute for the expertise of a lawyer, but it will help to make 
encounters with law and lawyers less mysterious.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Because the language of law can often seem to be a foreign tongue, the definitions in this dictionary are written in a style that as far as possible expresses unfamiliar legal concepts in ordinary English, without introducing inaccuracies caused by oversimplifica¬ tion.
text_raw:
Because the language of law can often seem to be a foreign 
tongue, the definitions in this dictionary are written in a style that 
as far as possible expresses unfamiliar legal concepts in ordinary 
English, without introducing inaccuracies caused by oversimplifica¬ 
tion.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: If an unfamiliar legal term occurs in a definition, the user can find it entered and defined at its own place in the dictionary.
text_raw:
If an unfamiliar legal term occurs in a definition, the user can 
find it entered and defined at its own place in the dictionary.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Fur¬ ther, any word that occurs in Merriam-Webster’s Dictionary of Law is entered either in this book or, if it is not a legal term, in a current edition of any of Merriam-Webster’s hardback or paperback adult dictionaries.

Fur¬ 
ther, any word that occurs in Merriam-Webster’s Dictionary of Law 
is entered either in this book or, if it is not a legal term, in a current

dictionaries.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: As a further aid in clarifying obscure terminology, extensive use is made throughout the book of verbal illustrations—often direct quo¬ tations from legal sources—demonstrating how words are actually used.

chapter_title: chapter 11 of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code.
text: Some bonds, such as fidelity bonds, function as insurance agreements, in which the surety promises to pay for financial loss caused by the bad behavior of an obligated person or by some contin¬ gency over which the person may have no control. appeal bond : a cost bond required by a rule of procedure (as Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 7) to be given by an appellant in order to cover the costs of an appeal appearance bond : an often unsecured bond given by a defendant in a crimi¬ nal trial to guarantee the defendant’s appearance in court as scheduled attachment bond 1 : a bond given by a plaintiff seeking to attach the defen¬ dant’s property that ensures payment to the defendant of any damages suffered because of the attachment in the event the plaintiff loses the suit 2 : a bond given by a defendant in order to have an attachment released that ensures pay¬ ment of a judgment awarded to the plaintiff bail bond : a bond given by a criminal defendant or by his or her surety to en¬ sure compliance with the terms of bail and esp. with the requirement that the defendant appear in court as scheduled bid bond : a surety bond often required of contractors bidding on construction work to ensure that the successful bidder will accept the job and will also provide a performance bond blanket bond : a fidelity bond covering all persons or all of a category of per¬ sons employed (as by a bank) or holding office (as of a trustee in bankruptcy) com*ple*tion bond :

chapter_title: chapter 12 n : chapter 12 of the U.S. Bank¬
text: Section (a) permits a class action if “(1) the class is so numerous that joinder of all mem¬ bers is impracticable, (2) there are ques¬ tions of law or fact common to the class, (3) the claims or defenses of the repre¬ sentative parties are typical of the claims or defenses of the class, and (4) the rep¬ resentative parties will fairly and ade¬ quately protect the interests of the class.” If the action satisfies these requirements, it must then fit into one of three catego¬ ries:

chapter_title: chapter 11 or 12 bankruptcy and has the
text: In section 1-201 of the Uniform Commercial Code, good faith is defined generally as “honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned.” Article 2 of the U.C.C. says “good faith in the case of a merchant means honesty in fact and the observance of reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing in the trade.” Similarly, Article 3 on nego¬ tiable instruments defines good faith as “honesty in fact and the observance of reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing,” a definition which also applies to the provisions of Article 4 on bank de¬ posits and collections and Article 4A on funds transfers.

text: While the writ no longer gov¬ erns civil pleading and has lost many of its applications, the extraordinary writs esp. of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohi¬ bition, and certiorari indicate its historical importance as an instrument of judicial authority. alias writ: a writ issued upon the failure of a previous one alternative writ : a writ commanding one to perform a mandated act or else to show cause why the act need not be performed — compare PEREMPTORY writ in this entry extraordinary writ : a writ granted as an extraordinary remedy at the discre¬ tion of the court in its jurisdiction over officials or inferior tribunals — called also prerogative writ; see also CER¬ TIORARI, HABEAS CORPUS, MANDAMUS, PROCEDENDO, PROHIBITION, QUO WAR¬ RANTO; compare WRIT OF RIGHT 2 in this entry 0 Extraordinary writs were originally writs exercised by royal prerogative. judicial writ: a writ issued by a court un¬ der its own seal for judicial purposes in the course of a proceeding or to enforce a judgment — compare ORIGINAL WRIT in this entry original writ : a writ formerly used in England that issued out of chancery as the means of bringing a suit and defen¬ dant before the court — compare JUDI¬ CIAL WRIT in this entry 0 The original writ was superseded by the summons in 1873. peremptory writ : a writ (as of man¬ damus) that presents an absolute order without the alternative to show cause (a peremptory writ of prohibition) — com¬ pare ALTERNATIVE WRIT in this entry prerogative writ Ypri-'ra-go-tivA : ex¬ traordinary WRIT in this entry writ of assistance 1 : a writ issued to a law officer (as a sheriff or marshal) for the enforcement of a court order or de¬ cree; esp : one used to enforce an order for the possession of lands 2 : a writ provided for under British rule in co¬ lonial America that authorized customs officers to search unspecified places for any smuggled goods 0 Many colonial courts refused to issue writs of assis¬ tance, which were a focus of bitter re¬ sentment against arbitrary searches and seizures.

Classifications of Law 
Law may be classified in several ways: by system (common and civil law), by source (constitu¬ 
tional, statutory, and case law), by the parties involved (public and private law), by substance (civil 
and criminal law), and by function (substantive and procedural law).

Each of these classifications

chapter_title: chapter 13 of the Bankruptcy Code.
text: Common Law and Civil Law Systems The two primary systems of American law are the common law system and the civil law system.
text_raw:
Common Law and Civil Law Systems 
The two primary systems of American law are the common law system and the civil law system.

chapter_title: chapter 13 of the Bankruptcy Code.
text: The common-law system, which developed in England, is the most prevalent system of law in North America.
text_raw:
The common-law system, which developed in England, is the most prevalent system of law in 
North America.

chapter_title: chapter 13 of the Bankruptcy Code.
text: The civil law system in North America is strongest in Louisiana in the United States and in Quebec in Canada; it is also prevalent in Mexico.
text_raw:
The civil law system in North America is strongest in Louisiana in the United 
States and in Quebec in Canada; it is also prevalent in Mexico.

chapter_title: chapter 13 of the Bankruptcy Code.
text: The common-law system is based on precedent and the principle of stare decisis.
text_raw: The common-law system is based on precedent and the principle of stare decisis.

chapter_title: chapter 13 of the Bankruptcy Code.
text: Although the legislative bodies at the federal, state, and local levels enact written statutes, and sometimes collect portions of those statutes into “codes,” there is no formal, comprehensive code of common law.
text_raw:
Although the 
legislative bodies at the federal, state, and local levels enact written statutes, and sometimes collect 
portions of those statutes into “codes,” there is no formal, comprehensive code of common law.

chapter_title: chapter 13 of the Bankruptcy Code.
text: Instead, the common law is stated in court decisions, and it is changed or modified by subsequent cases or statutes.
text_raw:
Instead, the common law is stated in court decisions, and it is changed or modified by subsequent 
cases or statutes.

chapter_title: chapter 13 of the Bankruptcy Code.
text: The civil law system may be traced back to the Roman law from which most European law systems originated.

The civil law system may be traced back to the Roman law from which most European law 
systems originated.

chapter_title: chapter 13 of the Bankruptcy Code.
text: It was brought to the Western Hemisphere by the French, Spanish, and Portu¬ guese.

chapter_title: chapter 13 of the Bankruptcy Code.
text: The civil law system as it exists in Europe is the result of Napoleon Bonaparte’s efforts: he provided for the drafting of the Code Civil or Code Napoleon, which restated the earlier principles of Roman law in more modem terms.

chapter_title: chapter 13 of the Bankruptcy Code.
text: In the civil law system, the Code Civil is a general statement of legal principles that is looked to in the interpretation of statutes and cases, and civilian courts do not follow the principle of stare decisis.

The electors shall meet in their respective states, and vote by ballot for President and Vice

a majority of the whole number of electors appointed; and if no person have such majority , then 
from the persons having the highest numbers not exceeding three on the list of those voted for as
